newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico rebels say numbers are growing fast.
newsitem.headline: Mexico rebels say numbers are growing fast.

text.p: Mexico's Marxist rebels said their numbers have been growing fast since they launched a rebellion nearly a year ago to topple the government of President Ernesto Zedillo.

Guerrillas from the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) told reporters on Saturday their ranks have swelled by about 60 percent since June 1996, when the previously unknown group announced its presence in western Guerrero state.

"Sympathy for our cause has grown, we can see it and feel it. More and more people are joining our ranks," a rebel leader, known as Captain Daniel, told a Reuters photographer and reporters from three Mexican newspapers.
"If I had to put a figure on how much our support has grown it would be by about 60 percent," he said. When asked if that included fighters, he said: "Yes."

Some 30 rebels dressed in olive military fatigues and carrying AK-47 assault rifles met with journalists in the remote hills bordering Guerrero's coastline between the resort city of Acapulco and the port of Lazaro Cardenas, 185 miles (300 km) southwest of Mexico City. The area is known as La Costa Grande, or Big Coast.

Captain Daniel would not reveal how many fighters the EPR has, although some reports have said the group has at least several hundred. Military experts do not rate it a serious threat to Mexico's army.

The rebels condemned the bloody end to Peru's recent hostage drama and held a minute of silence to honour the 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement guerrillas killed in the Peruvian military raid that rescued all but one of 72 hostages held by the Marxist rebels.

Also on Saturday, police in neighbouring Oaxaca said they arrested two local EPR leaders, Agustin and Adrian Pacheco, in La Sirena Loxicha, a Zapotec Indian community some 135 miles (210 km) south of Mexico City.
Villagers said the two men's father, 95-year-old Gaudencio Pacheco, died after being beaten by police during the arrest. They said a third local Indian was hauled away by police agents.

After launching a series of attacks in at least five Mexican states last year, in which at least 30 people died and 50 more injured, the group has declared a series of ceasefires to carry out what it terms "armed propaganda."
Rebels told reporters their peaceful acts have spurred keen interest among marginalized Indian villages in Guerrero, Oaxaca and a handful of other central Mexican states.

"Once we establish a military unit in an area, the sympathy begins ... We have seen a lot of young people joining our ranks ... and even the elderly want to fight. We have one unit with a grandfather, the son and the grandson," said another rebel leader, Commander Antonio.

The EPR's military command in Oaxaca said in a statement on Sunday that it had carried out eight acts of propaganda during April, including briefly occupying two towns to distribute leaflets and answer questions from local villagers about the armed movement.

Mexican President Zedillo has branded the EPR a "terrorist" organisation and has vowed to hunt down its members. Army and police have arrested hundreds of alleged EPR collaborators, although few have been formally charged.

The group has called for the overthrow of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party and the establishment of a government for the poor. Its proposals include nationalisation of the banks and a return to communal ownership of agricultural land.
